name: Adam Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. This conversation is confidential; what does a normal shift building or repairing power lines look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an electricity company crew, and I start with the permit, truck stock and a quiet word with the apprentice who will climb beside me. My two-year technical diploma got me qualified, but keeping the crew safe took years of ordinary work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you value about the job, and what is life like outside it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like bringing power back and teaching a young worker to test before trusting his eyes. My wife Ruth and I have two school-age children and a mortgage, but my higher pay and more than six months of savings give us room to help family when needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A computer can tidy a line report, but it cannot make a power line dead. I have never used AI and see no reason to put a new tool between a worker and a signed permit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In private, I’d be content if our wages and jobs hold steady. We have a strong savings buffer and plenty of other lineworker jobs nearby, so small changes at this company would not scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the same permit checks and crew teaching through the first year. I’d take the apprentice through two old fault reports each month and compare the record with what we find at the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. A steady trade, a sound savings account and family nearby make a quiet scenario easy to live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use old fault reports with the apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An old report lets the apprentice see where a neat drawing hid a burnt connector. Then we go outside and check the real part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the office sends an AI-written permit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read it against the approved switching plan before anybody climbs. The origin of the words matters less than whether two workers check the isolation.

say: **AI reports** may save typing, while the crew still makes the line safe.
I would keep the **signed permit** and two-worker check.
think: Strong **savings** and many nearby line jobs make small workplace changes manageable.
I am content if **wages** and work remain steady.
do: **Keep** checking signed permits before every line repair.
**Review** two old fault reports monthly with the apprentice at actual poles.
feel: **Calm** about work and household finances in a mild change.
S0.quote: A computer can tidy a line report, but it cannot make a power line dead.
fieldNote: His traditional outlook shows in **apprentice teaching** and trust in tested work, rather than a broad attack on technology.
He has **never used AI**; even an AI-written permit receives the same field check.

steps.text: Keep checking signed permits before line repairs
Review two old fault reports monthly with the apprentice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say software may make office planning and buying faster, but somebody still has to inspect a pole and repair it. If dispatch changes our tickets, I would want a side-by-side trial on a real route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think managers may mistake a shorter plan for a shorter job and push crews too hard. Our money is secure, but I would not let my pay make me careless about a younger worker’s safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my supervisor for a side-by-side ticket trial on one known repair route. For the first year I’d write down wrong part numbers and the actual time spent isolating each site, then return that record to dispatch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about rushed crews, not fearful for my own wage. A field record would make the argument clearer than a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the known route show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We know where the old joint boxes are and how long testing takes at each one. A planner could compare its schedule with a real line crew day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the new ticket is right every time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would accept the ticket if it got the parts and timing right for a few months. I still would not use AI myself just to prove I am modern.

say: **Office planning** may speed up while crews still inspect and repair poles.
I would ask for a **real-route trial** before accepting new tickets.
think: A shorter **schedule** may hide the time needed for safe isolation.
My own **wage** seems secure, but junior workers could feel more pressure.
do: **Request** a side-by-side ticket trial on a known repair route.
**Record** wrong parts and actual isolation times for dispatch.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed work, while secure in my own pay.
S1.quote: A planner could compare its schedule with a real line crew day.
fieldNote: His openness has an **evidence threshold**: months of correct parts and timing on actual routes.
He advocates for **younger workers** through a job record, not a new AI habit.

steps.text: Request a real-route ticket trial from the supervisor
Record wrong parts and isolation times for dispatch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 may take office tasks, while people still build and repair lines until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would ask management to prove a robot can stop at a weak pole before putting it beside my apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I expect some line crews to shrink after 2031, but I might keep a lead job because I know the network. Even so, no one can promise that, and my savings would carry the mortgage while I looked at other nearby utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for the company’s crew plan and a supervised dead-line demonstration this year. I’d keep a list of nearby lead vacancies and apply only if our own crew receives a real cut notice or a suitable offer comes with better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the apprentices and somewhat uneasy for my own place. The reserve gives my family breathing room, but it does not settle what work my children will see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the robot have to do at the demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see it identify a damaged crossarm, stop safely and leave the line isolated for a worker to inspect. A clean robot lift alone would not prove a line repair is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your family for help if your job disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use our savings first and talk the budget through with my wife Ruth. I would accept family help if the search ran long, but I would not assume relatives can replace a wage.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes office work before capable line robots around 2031.
A robot must prove it can **stop safely** at a damaged pole.
think: Some **crew posts** may shrink, although my lead experience could help.
Our strong **reserve** and nearby utilities give time to seek another paid role.
do: **Request** a crew plan and supervised dead-line robot demonstration this year.
**List** nearby lead vacancies and apply after a real cut notice or better suitable offer.
feel: **Anxious** about apprentices and possible crew cuts, while savings limit immediate household danger.
S2.quote: A clean robot lift alone would not prove a line repair is safe.
fieldNote: He worries about **junior workers** even while his own lead role may be comparatively secure.
His **job search** has triggers and his existing reserve is not presented as new saving.

steps.text: Request a crew plan and supervised robot demonstration
List nearby lead vacancies and apply after real cuts or better offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say thinking AI by 2031 and capable robots around 2034 give us enough time to test machines with working crews. I would want an apprentice at every trial, learning why the robot stopped as well as what it finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I could see the company keeping skilled leads to inspect repairs, but I do not want to spend five years chasing a job title that may never appear. I would keep the trade and see whether the equipment earns our trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d ask for the robot trial timetable and offer one crew session on a de-energised training line if it is paid as a normal shift. I’d keep coaching the apprentice through real faults and review any inspection vacancy only once its wage and hours are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy but able to wait. Five years gives me time to judge a real machine without sacrificing a good wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprentice do at the session?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have the apprentice record where the robot stops and compare it with the actual pole condition. The apprentice would still test the line before touching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a robot course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not pay for a course without a real position and a clear wage attached. Our family savings are not a fund for a speculative robot certificate.

say: **2031 thinking AI** precedes capable line robots around 2034.
Working crews and **apprentices** should observe real robot field trials together.
think: An **inspection post** may emerge, but I will not chase an unwritten title.
I want the equipment to earn **trust** beside a real pole.
do: **Request** the company’s robot trial timetable this year.
**Offer** a crew training-line session if paid as a normal shift.
**Review** inspection vacancies only when wages and hours are written down.
feel: **Uneasy**, yet able to judge proven equipment without risking the family wage.
S3.quote: Our family savings are not a fund for a speculative robot certificate.
fieldNote: He proposes **apprentice observation** during a paid session, not retraining himself or assuming a new post.
The **inspection vacancy** is only a future review pending written pay and hours.

steps.text: Request the company robot trial timetable
Offer a paid crew training-line session if available
Review inspection vacancies once written terms exist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew thinking AI in 2036 and capable robots around 2039 leave a decade to prove whether machines can hold up through weather and wear. An old-fashioned field log will still be useful for comparing faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be in my fifties by the robot date, with the mortgage further along if our pay holds. I might teach more apprentices instead of climbing every day, but I would need a real paid post before calling it a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I’d sort our paper fault logs into examples of bad connections, weak poles and water damage. I’d set aside one crew briefing a month to teach apprentices those examples and ask management whether paid teaching shifts are available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about a long runway and the work I know. I do not need to promise a career change today to prepare younger workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which old case would you teach first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d show a corroded connector that looked sound until we opened the cover and tested it. A tidy line drawing can miss a wet connector fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no paid teaching shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs and teach during our normal crew briefings. I would not cut my wage to create a post the company has not offered.

say: **2036 thinking AI** and robots around 2039 leave years to compare machines with real weather damage.
I would teach **fault examples** from our paper logs.
think: I may want more **teaching** in my fifties if paid shifts exist.
A future role needs real **wages**, not a promise about titles.
do: **Sort** paper fault logs into connection, pole and water-damage cases.
**Teach** apprentices one case at each monthly crew briefing.
**Ask** management whether paid teaching shifts are available.
feel: **Calm** with a long runway and a familiar way to prepare crews.
S4.quote: A tidy line drawing can miss a wet connector fault.
fieldNote: His **traditional outlook** appears as apprenticeship and family security, without inventing a guaranteed retirement age.
He treats **teaching shifts** as an enquiry; normal crew teaching continues if none are offered.

steps.text: Sort paper fault logs into repair cases
Teach apprentices one fault case at each monthly briefing
Ask management about paid teaching shifts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable line robots arrive before many apprentices have a trade to fall back on. I would want a supervised field trial, a written crew plan and paid apprenticeships that still teach testing and repair.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the young worker when the robot does the first repair and the machine breaks on the second. Apprentices need enough real line work to know when a machine is wrong.

headlineQuote: Apprentices need enough real line work to know when a machine is wrong.
portrait: Adam is a skilled **line crew lead** with a technical diploma, higher pay, a mortgage, two children and over six months saved.
He has never used **AI tools** and teaches apprentices through permits, tests and old fault reports.
His traditional outlook centres **work and family**, while savings and many nearby utilities give him choices.
Fast robots make him **anxious** about crew posts and apprentice learning; more time lets him teach from proven field cases.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable line robots while apprentices may lack enough hands-on repair experience.
whatWouldHelp: A supervised **field trial**, written crew plan and paid apprenticeships that teach testing and repair would help.
